A stream. It runs through the meadow, just beyond the edge of the wood. I can hear it from my perch. The water is cold, and the bank is muddy. I sometimes fly down to drink, but I always watch for owls. There are no owls near the stream, but I know the crows come to drink too. They are loud and messy. I do not like them.

I drink from the stream. I land on the bank, dip my beak into the water, and drink. Sometimes I drink from the dew on the leaves at dawn. I do not drink much, but I need to. The water is cold, and it keeps me strong. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Sometimes it sounds louder, when the rain falls or the leaves fall into it. I know when it's full or low, and I know when the fish are near. The stream is my guide, my companion. A stream. It runs through the meadow behind my tree, just beyond the lane. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones and the occasional splash of a fish. I don't drink from it, but I watch the owlets when they come down to drink. The stream is where the pebbles are, and where the jays come to bathe.

I can hear the mice scurrying under the grass, and sometimes the pheasants run across it. The meadow is where I hunt at night, and I can see the lights of the village from there. I sit on the edge of the stream, listening for the rustle of leaves and the tap of a mouse on the ground. Grassy place. That is the meadow, the one with the stream through it. I hunt there at dusk, when the light is thin and the mice come out. The grass is tall and green, and the stream makes a sound like a whisper. I sit on a branch above it and wait. The mice run in the grass, and I drop. The stream is cold, and I do not like it. I prefer the wood.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and run through the meadow at night. I hear them under the leaves and the grass, and I strike. They are the main reason I am awake at night. I eat them whole, bones and all, and I cache the bones in the hollow of the old oak.

My favourite prey is the pebble. Small, plump, and full of fat. I can hear them moving in the grass, and I can strike fast. They are easy to catch, and they taste good. I eat them often. I also eat mice, shrews, and earthworms. But the pebble is my favourite. I can hear them in the dark, and I can wait for them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, listening, and when I hear the rustle, I drop. The grass is soft, and I land silently. Sometimes I miss, but I wait. The grass is good cover, and the voles don't see me. I eat them whole, bones and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A shrew, a mouse, a pebble, a moth. I tear it with my teeth and swallow it whole. It goes down the gullet, and I feel it in my belly. I don't chew. I don't spit. I just swallow. It's how I eat. I don't know what it feels like to chew. I just swallow whole.

Shrews. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the lane. I hear them, and I drop. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them in the ivy, in the grass, sometimes in the lane itself. They are the most common. I eat them, and I eat them again.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest of feathers and dry leaves. I sleep there at night, and I watch the meadow from the top of the oak. The hollow is safe, and I have a view of the lane and the stream. I call from there, and I hear the owlets when they are hungry. The hollow is my home, and I have been there for many years.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, just beyond the stream. The bark is rough and the leaves fall in autumn. I have a hollow in the trunk, and I sleep in the dry part. The owlet is in the nest, and I watch the meadow from here. The stream is my boundary, and I do not cross it.

A hollow in the old oak, hollowed by wind and time. I have made a nest of dry leaves and feathers. The oak is hollowed on the right side, and I sit in the hollow with my head on the edge, looking out. The hollow is warm, and the leaves keep the rain out. I have a view of the meadow and the stream. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, hollowed by wind and time. The bark is rough and the wood smells of damp and moss. I have a nest of twigs and feathers, soft and warm. I sleep there at night, curled up, and I watch the meadow from the branches above. The hollow is safe, and the owls know it. I have been here for many years, and the wood has grown quieter as the trees have died. I do not move

A hollow in the old oak. I found it when I was a young owl, and it has kept me through the years. It is high up, where the branches are thick and the wind does not reach. I can hear the leaves rustle and the rain patter through the branches. The hollow is dark inside, but I have learned to see in the dark. I have a nest of twigs and feathers, and I have raised my young there. It is my home.
